exercises.passage:
Let Teenagers Sleep

Asking a sixteen-year-old to solve algebra at half past seven in the morning ignores biology. During puberty, the body clock shifts later: teenagers naturally feel sleepy later at night and need to sleep later in the morning. A schedule that suited a ten-year-old can leave an older student permanently short of rest.

The effects go beyond yawning in class. Studies link short sleep in teenagers to weaker concentration, lower mood, and more frequent illness. Some school districts that moved start times later by even one hour reported better attendance and calmer morning lessons within a single term.

Change is not simple. Bus timetables, parents' working hours, and after-school sports all depend on the current schedule. Still, the evidence points in one direction: when schools treat sleep as part of learning rather than an obstacle to it, students arrive more ready to learn.
